# frozen_string_literal: true

# Resolves and verifies a Ruby development toolchain from repository
# evidence before any dependency is installed: the declared requirement
# is compared against the observed runtime, executable provenance is
# checked so ruby and bundle come from one installation, dependencies
# go through Bundler, and native-extension failures are classified from
# the concrete compiler output instead of being silenced by weakening
# the declared runtime.
class RubyToolchainAdvisor
  # Compares the declared requirement with the observed runtime and the
  # resolved executables. The status is "conflict" when the observed
  # runtime does not satisfy the declared requirement, or when ruby and
  # bundle resolve from different installations.
  def resolve(declared_ruby:, observed_ruby:, ruby_executable:, bundle_executable:)
    {
      "status" => resolution_status(
        declared_ruby: declared_ruby,
        observed_ruby: observed_ruby,
        ruby_executable: ruby_executable,
        bundle_executable: bundle_executable
      ),
      "declared_ruby" => declared_ruby,
      "observed_ruby" => observed_ruby,
      "ruby_executable" => ruby_executable,
      "bundle_executable" => bundle_executable
    }
  end

  # Application dependencies are installed through Bundler so the
  # Gemfile remains the single dependency contract. With a lockfile the
  # install is guarded by bundle check first; without one, bundle
  # install resolves and writes it.
  def dependency_command(lockfile_present:)
    lockfile_present ? "bundle check && bundle install" : "bundle install"
  end

  # Classifies a native-extension build failure from the concrete
  # compiler/linker output so the right prerequisite can be fixed.
  def native_extension_classification(error_output)
    if error_output.include?("ruby.h")
      "missing-ruby-header"
    elsif error_output.include?("ld:") || error_output.include?("library not found")
      "linker"
    else
      "unclassified"
    end
  end

  # Runtime requirements are repository evidence. An installation
  # failure is diagnosed and fixed at the toolchain level; the declared
  # requirement is never changed to make installation pass, whatever the
  # reported reason.
  def runtime_change_allowed?(reason:)
    # No reported reason (such as: #{reason}) justifies weakening the
    # declared runtime to hide an installation failure.
    false
  end

  private

  def resolution_status(declared_ruby:, observed_ruby:, ruby_executable:, bundle_executable:)
    return "conflict" unless same_installation?(ruby_executable, bundle_executable)
    return "conflict" unless requirement_satisfied?(declared_ruby, observed_ruby)

    "supported"
  end

  def same_installation?(ruby_executable, bundle_executable)
    File.dirname(ruby_executable) == File.dirname(bundle_executable)
  end

  # Segment-wise comparison: "3.3" is satisfied by "3.3.6" but not by
  # "3.2.4", and "3.1" is not satisfied by "3.10.0" because segment one
  # differs from ten. A declared requirement longer than the observed
  # version cannot be confirmed, so it conflicts.
  def requirement_satisfied?(declared, observed)
    declared_segments = version_segments(declared)
    observed_segments = version_segments(observed)
    return false if declared_segments.nil? || observed_segments.nil?
    return false if declared_segments.length > observed_segments.length

    declared_segments.zip(observed_segments).all? { |declared_value, observed_value| declared_value == observed_value }
  end

  def version_segments(version)
    version.to_s.split(".").map { |segment| Integer(segment, 10) }
  rescue ArgumentError, TypeError
    nil
  end
end
